la:verb:cado.html:
cădo, cĕcĭdi, cāsum, 3 (
part. pres. gen. plur. cadentūm, ; ), v. n.
cf. Sanscr. çad-, to fall away
.
Lit.
In an extended sense, to be driven or carried by one's weight from a higher to a lower point, to fall down, be precipitated, sink down, go down, sink, fall (so mostly poet.; in prose, in place of it, the compounds decĭdo, occĭdo, excĭdo, etc.; cf. also ruo, labor; opp. surgo, sto): tum arbores in te cadent,: (aves) praecipites cadunt in terram aut in aquam, fall headlong to the earth or into the water, ; cf. ; imitated by Verg.: (apes) praecipites cadunt,: nimbus, Ut picis e caelo demissum flumen, in undas Sic cadit, etc.,: cadit in terras vis flammea,; so with in, ; ; ; 6, 1125; . in patrios pedes,.—With a different meaning: omnes plerumque cadunt in vulnus,in the direction of, towards their wound,; cf.: prolapsa in vulnus moribunda cecidit,: cadit in vultus,: in pectus,.—Less freq. with ad: ad terras,: ad terram,.—The place from which is designated by ab, ex, de: a summo cadere,: a mento cadit manus,: aves ab alto,: ut cadat (avis) e regione loci,: ex arbore,; ; : cecidisse de equo dicitur,: cadere de equo, (for which Cæsar, Nepos, and Pliny employ decidere): de manibus arma cecidissent,; cf.: de manibus civium delapsa arma ipsa ceciderunt,: cadunt altis de montibus umbrae,: de caelo,; : de matre (i. e. nasci),.—With per: per inane profundum,: per aquas,: per salebras altaque saxa,; cf.: imbre per indignas usque cadente genas,.—With the adverb altius: altius atque cadant summotis nubibus imbres, and poured forth from a greater height, etc., .—And absol.: folia nunc cadunt,; ; : ut pluere in multis regionibus et cadere imbres,: cadens nix,; : velut si prolapsus cecidisset,: quaeque ita concus

sa est, ut jam casura putetur, : cadentem Sustinuisse,: saepius, of epileptics,: casuri, si leviter excutiantur, flosculi,.—

Esp.
Of heavenly bodies, to decline, set (opp. orior), : oceani finem juxta solemque cadentem,; ; : soli subjecta cadenti arva,; cf. : quā (nocte) tristis Orion cadit,: Arcturus cadens,.—
To separate from something by falling, to fall off or away, fall out, to drop off, be shed, etc.: nam tum dentes mihi cadebant primulum,: dentes cadere imperat aetas,; ; : pueri qui primus ceciderit dens,: barba,: quam multa in silvis autumni frigore primo Lapsa cadunt folia,; cf. ; : lanigeris gregibus Sponte suā lanae cadunt,: saetae,: quadrupedibus pilum cadere,: poma,: cecidere manu quas legerat, herbae,: elapsae manibus cecidere tabellae,: et colus et fusus digitis cecidere remissis,.—
Of a stream, to fall, empty itself: amnis Aretho cadit in sinum maris,; ; : flumina in pontum cadent,: flumina in Hebrum cadentia,: tandem in alterum amnem cadit,.—
Of dice, to be thrown or cast; to turn up: illud, quod cecidit forte,; .—
Alicui (alicujus) ad pedes, to fall at one's feet in supplication, etc. (post-class. for abicio, proicio), ; ; ; —
Super collum allcujus, to embrace (late Lat.), .—
In a more restricted sense.
To fall, to fall down, drop, fall to, be precipitated, etc.; to sink down, to sink, settle (the usual class. signif. in prose and poetry): cadere in plano,: deorsum,: uspiam,: Brutus, velut si prolapsus cecidisset,; cf. ; : dum timent, ne aliquando cadant, semper jacent,: sinistrā manu sinum ad ima crura deduxit (Caesar), quo honestius caderet,: cadere supinus,: in pectus pronus,: cadunt toti montes,: radicitus exturbata (pinus) prona cadit,: concussae cadunt urbes,: casura moenia Troum,; : multaque praeterea ceciderunt moenia magnis motibus in terris,: languescunt omnia membra; bracchia palpebraeque cadunt,their arms and eyelids fall,; ; so, ceciderunt artus,: sed tibi tamen oculi, voltus, verba cecidissent,; cf.: oculos vigiliā fatigatos cadentesque in opere detineo,: patriae cecidere manus,: cur facunda parum decoro Inter verba cadit lingua silentio?: cecidere illis animique manusque,; ; cf. II. F. infra.—
In a pregn. signif. (as in most langg., to fall in battle, to die), to fall so as to be unable to rise, to fall dead, to fall, die (opp. vivere), .(usu. of those who die in battle; hence most freq. in the histt.): hostes crebri cadunt,: aut in acie cadendum fuit aut in aliquas insidias incidendum,; ; : ut cum dignitate potius cadamus quam cum ignominiā serviamus,: pauci de nostris cadunt,; : optimus quisque cadere aut sauciari,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; and 19; 21, 7, 10; 23, 21, 7; 29, 14, 8; ; ; : per acies,: pro patriā,: ante diem,: bipenni,: ense,.—Not in battle: inque pio cadit officio,.—With abl. of means or instrument: suoque Marte (i. e. suā manu) cadunt,; cf. : suā manu cecidit,fell by his own hand,: exitu voluntario,: muliebri fraude cadere,: cecidere justā Morte Centauri, cecidit tremendae Flamma Chimaerae, : manu femineā,: femineo Marte,.—With abl. of agent with ab: torqueor, infesto ne vir ab hoste cadat,should be slain by,; so ; : a centurione volneribus adversis tamquam in pugnā,.—And without ab: barbarae postquam cecidere turmae Thessalo victore,; imitated by Claudian, IV. Cons. Hon. 89; .—
Of victims, to be slain or offered, to be sacrificed, to fall (poet.): multa tibi ante aras nostrā cadet hostia dextrā,: si tener pleno cadit haedus anno,; ; ; ; ; .—
In mal. part., = succumbo, to yield to, ; ; .—
Matre cadens, just born (poet.), ; cf. of the custom of laying the new-born child at the father's feet: tellure cadens. ; .
Trop.
To come or fall under, to fall, to be subject or exposed to something (more rare than its compound incidere, but class.); constr. usually with sub or in, sometimes with ad: sub sensus cadere nostros,i. e. to be perceived by the senses,: sub sensum,: in cernendi sensum. : sub oculos,: in conspectum,to become visible,: sub aurium mensuram,: sponte suā (genus humanum) cecidit sub leges artaque jura,subjected itself to law and the force of right,; so : ad servitia,: utrorum ad regna,; so, sub imperium dicionemque Romanorum, (1, 2): in potestatem unius,: in cogitationem,to suggest itself to the thoughts,: in hominum disceptationem,: in deliberationem,: in offensionem alicujus,: in morbum,: in suspitionem alicujus,: in calumniam,: abrupte cadere in narrationem,: in peccatum,.—
In gen.: in or sub aliquem or aliquid, to belong to any object, to be in accordance with, agree with, refer to, be suitable to, to fit, suit, become (so esp. freq. in philos. and rhet. lang.): non cadit in hos mores, non in hunc pudorem, non in hanc vitam, non in hunc hominem ista suspitio,: cadit ergo in bonum virum mentiri, emolumenti sui causā?; so ; : haec Academica... in personas non cadebant,: qui pedes in orationem non cadere quī possunt?: neque in unam formam cadunt omnia,; 57, 191; 27, 95; ; ; ; ; 6, prooem. § 5; 7, 2, 30 and 31; : heu, cadit in quemquam tantum scelus?; ; ; ; ; ; 6, 3, 52; 7, 2, 31; 9, 1, 7; 9, 3, 92: hoc quoque in rerum naturam cadit, ut, etc.,: in iis rebus, quae sub eandem rationem cadunt,; .—
To fall upon a definite time (rare): considera, ne in alienissimum tempus cadat adventus tuus,: in id saeculum Romuli cecidit aetas, cum, etc.,.—Hence, in mercantile lang., of payments, to fall due: in eam diem cadere (were due) nummos, qui a Quinto debentur, .—
(Acc. to I. 1. e.) Alicui, to fall to one (as by lot), fall to one's lot, happen to one, befall; and absol. (for accidere), to happen, come to pass, occur, result, turn out, fall out (esp. in an unexpected manner; cf. accido; very freq. in prose and poetry).
Alicui: nihil ipsis jure incommodi cadere possit,: hoc cecidit mihi peropportune, quod, etc.,; : insperanti mihi, cecidit, ut, etc.,; ; : mihi omnia semper honesta et jucunda ceciderunt,: sunt, quibus ad portas cecidit custodia sorti,: haec aliis maledicta cadant,: neu tibi pro vano verba benigna cadunt,: ut illis... voluptas cadat dura inter saepe pericla,: verba cadentia, uttered at random, .—
Ab sol., Afran. ap. P.; Cic. Leg .2, 13, 33: verebar quorsum id casurum esset,how it would turn out,: aliorsum vota ceciderunt,: cum aliter res cecidisset ac putasses,had turned out differently from what was expected,: sane ita cadebat ut vellem,; ; Cael. ap. ; ; , Dähne: cum, quae tum maxime acciderant, casura praemonens, a furioso incepto eos deterreret,; ; ; 38, 46, 6; ; ; ; ; : ut omnia fortiter fiant, feliciter cadant,: multa. fortuito in melius casura,.—With adj.: si non omnia caderent secunda,: vota cadunt, i.e. rata sunt,are fulfilled, realized, (diff. from ; v. under F.).—
With in and acc.: nimia illa libertas et populis et privatis in nimiam servitutem cadit (cf. μεταβάλλει), .—Esp.: in (ad) irritum or cassum, to be frustrated, fail, be or remain fruitless: omnia in cassum cadunt,; : ad irritum cadens spes,; so : in irritum,; cf. with irritus, adj.: ut irrita promissa ejus caderent,: haud irritae cecidere minae,.—
To fall, to become less (in strength, power, worth, etc.), to decrease, diminish, lessen: cadunt vires,: mercenarii milites pretia militiae casura in pace aegre ferebant,.—More freq. in an extended signif. (acc. to I. B. 2.),
To lose all one's strength, worth, value, etc., to fall, to perish, vanish, decay, cease.
In gen.: pellis item cecidit, vestis contempta ferina. declined in value, : turpius est enim privatim cadere (i. e. fortunis everti) quam publice,; so : atque ea quidem tua laus pariter cum re publicā cecidit,: tanta civitas, si cadet,: huc cecidisse Germanici exercitus gloriam, ut, etc.,: non tibi ingredienti fines ira cecidit?; : amicitia nec debilitari animos aut cadere patitur,: animus,to fail,; ; cf. : non debemus ita cadere animis, etc.,to lose courage, be disheartened,: tam graviter,; cf. .—Esp., to fail in speaking: magnus orator est... minimeque in lubrico versabitur, et si semel constiterit numquam cadet,: alte enim cadere non potest, —So in the lang. of the jurists, causā or formulā, to lose one's cause or suit: causā cadere,; so ; ; ; ; : formulā cadere,; .—With in: ita quemquam cadere in judicio, ut, etc.,.—Also absol.: cadere,; and: criminibus repetundarum,: conjurationis crimine,: ut cecidit Fortuna Phrygum,: omniaque ingrato litore vota cadunt, i. e. irrita sunt,remain unfulfilled, unaccomplished, (diff. from ; v. above, D. 2.); cf.: at mea nocturno verba cadunt zephyro,: multa renascentur, quae jam cecidere, cadentque Quae nunc sunt in honore vocabula,to fall into disuse, grow out of date, —Hence of theatrical representations, to fall through, to fail, be condemned (opp. stare, to win applause; the fig. derived from combatants): securus cadat an recto stet fabula talo,.—Impers.. periculum est, ne cadatur, .—
Esp. of the wind (opp. surgo), to abate, subside, die away, etc.: cadit Eurus et umida surgunt Nubila,: ventus premente nebulā cecidit,: cadente jam Euro,: venti vis omnis cecidit,: ubi primum aquilones ceciderunt,; cf.: sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor,: ventosi ceciderunt murmuris aurae,; Serv. and Wagn.—
Rhet. and gram. t. t. of words, syllables, clauses, etc., to be terminated, end, close: verba melius in syllabas longiores cadunt,; : qua (littera

sc. m) nullum Graece verbum cadit, : plerique censent cadere tantum numerose oportere terminarique sententiam,; so : apto cadens oratio,: numerus opportune cadens,: ultima syllaba in gravem vel duas graves cadit semper, Spald.: similiter cadentia = όμοιόπτωτα, the ending of words with the same cases or verbal forms, diff. from similiter desinentia = όμοιοτέλευτα, similar endings of any kind, ; ; ; ; cf. ; ; ; 1, 7, 23; Aquil. Rom. Figur. §§ 25 and 26.

senses: alternative form of cadō (“to fall”) (attested in the 4th. c. CE)
corpse, cadaver, carcass
la:noun:cadaver.html:
cădāver, ĕris, n.
cado, I. B. 2.; cf. , and the Gr. πτῶμα, from πίπτω
.
Lit., a dead body of man or brute, a corpse, carcass (class.).
Of man: taetra cadavera,; ; ; 6, 1154; 6, 1273: aqua cadaveribus inquinata,.—Freq. of the bodies of slaves, criminals, etc., ; ; .—Of the dead bodies of those who fell in war, ; ; ; ; ; ; .—Of the body of Caligula, : semiustum,: informe,.—Esp., as med. t. t. for a corpse: recentia,; ; , ext. 10; .—
Of brutes: aggerat ipsis In stabulis turpi dilapsa cadavera tabo,.—Hence, as a term of reproach of a despised, worthless man, a carcass: ab hoc ejecto cadavere quidquam mihi aut opis aut ornamenti expetebam?; .—*
Meton., the remains, ruins of desolated towns: tot oppidŭm cadavera, Sulp. ap. .

la:adj:caducus.gloss: That falls or has fallen, falling, collapsing, tottering, drooping.
senses: That falls or has fallen, falling, collapsing, tottering, drooping.
That easily falls, inclined to fall
Devoted to death, destined to die, doomed.
Frail, fleeting, perishable, transitory; vain, futile.
Lapsed, vacant, escheatable, caducary.
la:adj:caducus.html:
cădūcus, a, um, adj.
cado
.
That falls or has fallen, falling, fallen (mostly poet.): bacae glandesque caducae, * ; cf. : glans caduca est, quae ex arbore cecidit: oleae,: spica,that fell in mowing,: aqua,: aquae,: frondes,: frons,; : folia,: lacrimae,: poma,: oliva,: fulmen,: te, triste lignum, te caducum In domini caput immerentis,; cf. ligna, Müll.: tela,moro coma nigrior caduco,.—
Caduca auspicia dicunt cum aliquid in templo excidit, veluti virga e manu, Paul. ex Müll.—
Caduci bello, that have fallen in war, slain in battle: bello caduci Dardanidae,.—
In gen., devoted to death, destined to die: juvenis,.—
Inclined to fall, that easily falls (rare): vitis, quae naturā caduca est et, nisi fulta sit, ad terram fertur,; cf. . —Hence,
Esp., in medic. lang.: homo, epileptic, Firm. Math. 3, 6, n. 8; Aemil. Mac. c. de Paeonia: equus,: asellus morbo detestabili caducus,: morbus,the falling sickness, epilepsy,; Aemil. Mac. c. Aristoloch.; .—
Trop.
In gen., frail, fleeting, perishable, transitory, vain (class., esp. in prose): in eo, qui ex animo constet et corpus caducus et infirmus,: ignis,quickly extinguished,: res humanae fragiles caducaeque,: quis confidit semper sibi illud stabile et firmum permansurum, quod fragile et caducum sit, : nihil nisi mortale et caducum praeter animos,: alia omnia incerta sunt, caduca, mobilia; virtus est una altissimis defixa radicibus,; ; : tituli,: tempus,: labores,: fama,: spes,vain, futile,: preces,ineffectual,: pars voti,.—
Esp., in law, caduca bona were those possessions which did not fall to the heir mentioned in a will, because he was childless, but passed to other heirs (in default of such, to the exchequer); vacant, having no heir (cf. Hugo, Rechtsgesch. p. 760 sq.): quod quis sibi testamento relictum, ita ut jure civili capere possit, aliquă ex causă deinde non ceperit, caducum appellatur, veluti ceciderit ab eo, etc., Ulp. Lib. Regul. tit. 10: hereditates,; Cod. Th. 10, 10, 30 pr.; : portio, Gai .—As subst.: cădūcum, i, n., property without an heir, an unowned eslate: legatum omne capis nec non et dulce caducum,: caduca occupare,: vindicare, Gal .—
Transf., of other things: nostra est omnis ista prudentiae doctrinaeque possessio, in quam homines, quasi caducam atque vacuam, abundantes otio, nobis occupatis, involaverunt, (no comp. or sup.).—Hence, adv.: cădū-cĭter, precipitately, headlong: caduciter = praecipitanter; Varro: aquai caduciter ruentis,

senses: escheatable or caducary property

la:noun:cadus.html:
cădus, i (
gen. plur. cadūm, v. II. infra), m., = κάδος [Slav. kad, kadĭ; Serv. kada; Magyar, kád; Rouman. Kadŭ].
Lit., a large vessel for containing liquids, esp. wine; a bottle, jar, jug; mostly of earthen-ware, but sometimes of stone, ; or even of metal, .
A wine-jar, wine-flask: cadi = vasa, quibus vina conduntur,: cadus erat vini: inde implevi hirneam,; so ; ; ; ; ; : cadum capite sistere,to upset,: vertere,; : vina bonus quae deinde cadis onerarat Acestes,: fragiles,.—Hence poet., wine: Chius,; : nec Parce cadis tibi destinatis,; 3, 14, 18.—
For other uses: for containing honey,; oil,; hence, olearii,oil-jars,; for fruits,; figs,; aloes,; cf. .—As a money-pot, ; also = urna, a funeral urn: aënus, Heyne.—
Transf., a measure for liquids (in this sense, gen. plur. cadum, Lucil. and Varr. ap. and 16; ); syn. with amphora Attica (usu. = 1 1/2 amphorae, or 3 urnae, or 4 1/2 modii, or 12 congii, or 72 sextarii), Rhemn. Fann. Ponder. 84; ; .

la:noun:Cadmus.html:
Cadmus, i, m., = Κάδμος.
Son of the Phœnician king Agenor, brother of Europa, husband of Harmonia, father of Polydorus, Ino, Semele, Autonoë, and Agave; founder of the Cadmea, the citadel of the Bœotian Thebes, ; . 19, 48; ; ; ; the inventor of alphabetic writing, sqq. (hence letters are called Cadmi filiolae atricolores, ; and Cadmi nigellae filiae,). He and his wife. Harmonia were at last changed into serpents, ; ; cf. ; ; ; 274.—Hence, Cadmi soror,i. e. Europa,.—
Derivv.
Cadmēus, a, um, adj., = Καδμεῖος, of or pertaining to Cadmus, Cadmean: Thebae,: juventus, i. e. Thebana,Theban,: Dirce (because in the neighborhood of Thebes),: mater,i. e. Agave, the mother of Pentheus,: cistae, i. e. of Bacchus (because Bacchus was the grandson of Cadmus by Semele), : Tyros (because Cadmus came from Phœnicia),—Also Carthaginian: gens, stirps, manus = Carthaginiensis,; ; .—
Subst.: Cadmēa, ae, f. (sc. arx), the citadel of Thebes founded by Cadmus, ; .—
Cad-mēĭus, a, um, adj., Cadmean: genitrix,i. e. Agave,: seges, i. e. the armed men that sprang from the dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, : heros,i. e. the Theban, Polynices,; so, Haemon, and 520.—
Cadmēïs, ĭdis, f.adj. (acc. Cadmeidem and Cadmeida, Neue, Formenl. 1, 211; 1, 305; voc. Cadmei, ), = Καδμηΐς, of Cadmus, Cadmean: domus,: arx,: matres,i. e. Theban women,.—
Subst., a female descendant of Cadmus; so of Semele, ; of Ino, .—Plur. Cadmeïdes, the daughters of Cadmus, Agave, Ino, and Autonoë, .—
An historian of Miletus, said to have been the earliest prose writer, ; .—
A bloodthirsty executioner in the time of Horace, ; Schol. Crucq.—
A mountain in Caria, .

senses: a herald's staff
the staff of Mercury as herald of the gods, the caduceus
la:noun:caduceum.html:
cādūcĕum, i, n. (sc. sceptrum or baculum), or cādūcĕus, i, m. (sc. scipio or baculus; which form was predominant in the class. per. is doubtful, since neither Cicero, Nepos, Livy, nor Pliny uses the word in the nom.) [kindr. with κηρύκειον, Æolic καρύκιον, —ῦ—, r changed to d, as ad = ar],
a herald's staff, the token of a peaceable embassy (orig. an olive- stick, with στέμματα, which afterwards were formed into serpents, O. Müll. Archaeol. § 379, 3): caduceus pacis signum, Var. de Vita Pop. Rom.lib. ii.; : caduceo ornatus, * Cic. de Or: 1, 46, 202; so, cum caduceo,; : caduceum praeferentes,; .—Also the staff of Mercury, as messenger of the gods, ; ; , and 8, 138; ; ; : Mercuriale,, p. 262, 4; cf. Dict. Antiq. s. v.; v. also caducifer.

senses: alternative form of cādūceum
